Mostly speculation follows, but I hypothesize that it's possible via two sensory processes: pattern following and distinction from noise.

First, we're capable of easily identifying distinct sensory inputs from even very noisy backgrounds: consider how easy it would be for you to see a green ball even in a pit full of red balls, or to smell popcorn or coffee even in a scented candle shop. In the same way, you can pretty easily hear a distinct voice from that of a crowd, especially if you already know the speaker or he/she has a particularly distinctive voice.

But of course, that can't explain the whole process, as you can do this even in a room full of strangers who all have similar sounding voices (though it would probably be a lot harder). Hence pattern following: even in the absence of distinction, we are able to focus our attention on a particular pattern and follow it more easily. For example, imagine a dozen or so flies buzzing about in front of you. Normally, this would seem completely chaotic, but if you focus your attention on a single one of the flies, you can follow its movement even through the crowd. Similarly, once you recognize the pattern of a voice and the words in its phrases, you begin to foresee the rest and listen for it, so to speak.

Neat bit odd trivia... some people can't do this very well. I've always had trouble making out conversation in areas where there was a lot of talking or music. At one point I had a hearing test as part of a comprehensive physical and was diagnosed with a deficiency in this area. The sound portion of my brain can't filter out ambient sound very well.

God if you can figure this out you'll become the next millionaire hearing aid creator. I worked with a professor that's developing a directional microphone inorder to improve hearingaids: http://research.binghamton.edu/Innovation/Featured_Faculty/Ron_Miles.php

This is dubbed the Cocktail party effect.

The cocktail party effect works best as a binaural effect, which requires hearing with both ears. People with only one functioning ear seem much more distracted by interfering noise than people with two healthy ears. The binaural aspect of the cocktail party effect is related to the localization of sound sources. The auditory system is able to localize at least two sound sources and assign the correct characteristics to these sources simultaneously. As soon as the auditory system has localized a sound source, it can extract the signals of this sound source out of a mixture of interfering sound sources.
